Version 1.0 
| Page 4 
 
1. 
Introduction/Overview  
 
South East Technological University (SETU) is committed to ensuring the highest levels of 
responsible practice of research in its community. Seeking knowledge, and imparting this 
knowledge are fundamental functions of higher education. It follows from the freedom to 
pursue knowledge that researchers working under the auspices of SETU have a moral 
obligation to society as well as the University to perform ethically conducted research with 
integrity. Observance of the highest standards of integrity must underlie all decisions and 
actions related to research. Research undertaken under the auspices of the University must 
also meet the highest ethical standards and must be in accordance with relevant Irish and EU 
law. Researchers must refrain from any conduct or action in their research practice in SETU 
that would breach these standards and unjustifiably detract from the good name of the 
institution and the relevant professional body to which they may belong.  
 
This document is guided by a number of policies both nationally and internationally.  
Nationally there is the National Policy Statement on Ensuring Research Integrity in Ireland2, a 
policy statement that provides Irish researchers with guidelines on how to perform research 
with the highest levels of integrity. This policy statement is supported and was developed 
through the National Research Integrity Forum. The Higher Education Authority (HEA) also 
compiled a set of principles titled HEA Principles of Good Research Practice in Irish HEIs3 that 
clearly focuses on the promotion of good practice in research and are directed at the 
institutional level. The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity4 was developed by 
All European Academies (ALLEA) and serves the European research community as a 
framework for self-regulation across all scientific and scholarly disciplines and for all research 
settings. The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity outlines a number of principles 
of good research practice which are to be observed by all researchers and research 
organisations, and these principles have been incorporated into SETU’s Code of Conduct for 
Responsible Research Practice. This document encompasses both national and European 
guidance on good research practice.  
2. 
Purpose 
 
This document outlines SETU’s Code of Conduct for Responsible Research Practice which 
includes its principles, practices and procedures. This code of conduct collates all relevant

SETU policies and procedures that govern the research process, and which collectively 
support an environment of responsible conduct of research. This policy document gives SETU 
researchers an overview of relevant Irish and EU legislation and regulations that affect 
research integrity. This code of conduct should be used in conjunction with other SETU 
policies which are referenced throughout this document, and which can be accessed from the 
SETU website.  
 
There is an onus on all SETU staff and students who carry out research to ensure that they are 
familiar with this Code of Conduct in conjunction with other relevant existing policies and 
procedures of SETU.   
3. 
Scope 
 
This Code of Conduct for Responsible Research Practice is applicable to all individuals and 
groups who carry out or support research activities under the auspices of SETU. This Code of 
Conduct applies to all permanent, part-time or contract staff employed by SETU engaged in 
research, or in the setting of research priorities, strategies, policies and the assessment of 
research on any SETU campuses or on behalf of SETU at any location (including secondments 
to other higher-level institutions).  
 
This includes: 
● 
All enrolled students at the University, 
● 
Full and part-time staff of the University, 
● 
All research staff, including postdoctoral researchers and research fellows, 
● 
All visiting and seconded staff and students,  
● 
Holders of associated, adjunct and emeritus positions, 
● 
Internal and external supervisors of postgraduate and undergraduate 
students, 
● 
Postgraduate and undergraduate students, 
● 
Contractors, sub-contractors, external collaborators and industrial 
partners involved in research-related activities, 
● 
Technical, professional, managerial, administrative and all support staff 
involved in research-related activities,  
● 
All individuals engaged in the setting of research priorities, strategies, 
policies and the assessment of research.

The term SETU Researcher shall be used throughout this document to refer to any or all of 
the above categories, as appropriate.  
4. 
Principles of Research Integrity  
 
SETU endorses a number of basic principles that underpin all good research practices. These 
principles are specified in the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (2023, p.5) 
and the National Policy Statement on Ensuring Research Integrity in Ireland (2024, p.4).  
 
These principles are as follows: 
• Reliability: in ensuring the quality of research, reflected in the design, methodology, 
analysis and use of resources. 
• Honesty: in developing, undertaking, reviewing, reporting and communicating 
research in a transparent, fair, full and unbiased way. 
• Respect: for colleagues, research participants and subjects, be they human or animal, 
society, ecosystems, cultural heritage and the environment. 
• Accountability: for the research from idea to publication, for its management and 
organisation, for training, supervision and mentoring, and for its wider impacts. 
      
All research conducted in SETU must be consistent with the above principles and with Irish 
and EU law, including national licensing requirements (e.g. export controls), and related SETU 
policies and procedures.  
5. 
Definitions  
 
The following are some identified core definitions used in this document. These include: 
 
Research integrity: refers to all the factors that underpin good research practice and 
promotes trust and confidence in the research process. Research integrity covers all 
disciplines of research and all sectors where research is carried out. Research integrity covers 
all research and the whole lifecycle of research, from the initial idea and design of the project, 
the writing of the proposal and application for funding, through to the conduct of the research 
and its dissemination. Research integrity should also ensure that environments and systems 
for research safeguard and enhance good research practice, rather than hinder it – which is 
often described as the ‘research culture‘.  
 
Research ethics: the process which ensures that, when engaging in research with human 
participants or using experimental animal models, all researchers engage in good practices 
that protects all such participants/subjects.

Research misconduct: can be defined as behaviours that deliberately or recklessly fall short 
of standards expected in the conduct of research. An offence constitutes research misconduct 
if it affects the integrity of the research record. The most serious misconduct behaviours 
include fabrication, falsification, or plagiarism in proposing, performing, or reviewing 
research, or in reporting research results. However, there are also other unacceptable 
research practices that seriously deviate from those that are commonly accepted within the 
research community for proposing, conducting, or reporting research, and serious or 
repeated examples of such practices can constitute research misconduct. Research 
misconduct does not include honest error or honest differences in the design, execution, 
interpretation or judgment in evaluating research methods or results, or misconduct 
unrelated to the research process. Similarly, it does not include poor research per se unless 
there is an intention to deceive.  
 
Research Integrity Officer: The Research Integrity Officer (RIO) is an employee of SETU. The 
RIO receives allegations of research misconduct. The RIO initiates and oversees the 
procedures for investigating allegations of research misconduct and ensures the 
confidentiality of the process. The RIO supports good research practices at SETU through 
policies, training and other supports. The RIO oversees mandatory research integrity training 
and is responsible for providing advice to researchers on research integrity related concerns. 
 
SETU Researcher: staff and students of SETU - including those with positions as 
emeritus/emerita staff, visiting scholars and those with adjunct status – who are engaged in 
research activities.     
6. 
Roles and Responsibilities  
 
SETU commits to: 
 
6.1 Supporting a research environment underpinned by a culture of integrity and based on   
good governance, a research environment that is inclusive, equitable and supportive, 
protecting the well-being of researchers; 
6.2 Ensuring that readily accessible policies, procedures and systems are in place to support 
and reinforce the responsible conduct of research; 
6.3 Providing SETU researchers with access to training, resources and support to ensure that 
they are aware of their obligations in respect of SETU policies and procedures related to 
responsible research practices and can comply with them. 
 
SETU Researchers commit to:

6.4 Carrying out research according to the standards of the Code of Conduct for Responsible 
Research Practice; 
6.5 Making themselves aware of and ensuring that all relevant requirements of Irish and EU 
law, all relevant SETU policies and procedures and the requirements of funding bodies are 
met, and to seek guidance from SETU when necessary; 
6.7 Ensuring they have completed mandatory research integrity training and any required 
refresher training to comply with their responsible conduct of research obligations. 
 
SETU’s RIO commits to: 
 
• Investigating research misconduct allegations received in writing and providing 
support and advice to SETU researchers on SETU policies, procedures and training 
related to research integrity and responsible research practices. 
7. 
Research Ethics 
 
All SETU researchers carrying out research involving humans and animals have a responsibility 
to meet the ethical requirements in the conduct of their research and to acquire ethical 
approval from the Research Ethics Committee (REC) before commencing their research.  
 
It is the responsibility of the REC to scrutinise and approve ethical applications for all research 
involving humans and animals to ensure research is compliant with statutory and ethical 
requirements and is conducted to the highest ethical principles.  
 
Researchers should refer to SETU’s Research Ethics Committee Operations and Application 
Guidance Documentation which clearly lays out the operation principles of SETU’s REC and 
provides guidance to those applying for approval.  Researchers should refer to the SETU 
Research Ethics webpage to access the Research Ethics Committee Operations and 
Application Guidance Documentation, to see the full list of research areas that require ethical 
approval and to download other relevant documentation including the SETU Ethical Approval 
Application Form.  
 
All researchers who wish to submit an application for ethical approval to the REC must also 
complete Research Integrity training and submit their certificate of completion to the REC as 
part of their application (see Section 9 Research Integrity Training).

8. 
Research Integrity Training 
 
SETU is committed to providing training, resources and supports to SETU researchers to 
ensure they are aware of their obligations in respect of research integrity. To fulfil this 
commitment SETU provides access to an online Research Integrity training package.  
 
It is mandatory for all SETU researchers to complete the Research Integrity training. 
Completion of the Research Integrity training is a mandatory requirement for holding a grant from 
many Irish research funding agencies and for acquiring ethical approval from SETU’s REC (see 
Section 8). It is also a requirement that all postgraduate research students complete the 
research integrity training during the first 12 months following their initial registration.  
 
SETU recommends that the Research Integrity training should be repeated at least every five 
years as recommended in the National Policy Statement for Research Integrity in Ireland5. 
This recommendation applies to all SETU researchers. 
 
SETU researchers are responsible for downloading and retaining their certificate of 
completion for presenting in case of an internal audit and as required by the REC and any 
external funding agencies. 
 
The Research Integrity training is available for all staff and students on SETU’s Virtual Learning 
Environments (VLEs). As part of the research integrity training, there are 8 online core 
modules and 5 specialist modules. Researchers must complete all 8 core modules. For 
information on how to access this training and the different modules that are available as part 
of it, researchers should refer to SETU’s research integrity webpage. 
 
In addition to the Research Integrity Training, all SETU postgraduate research students must 
complete a mandatory Universal Pathway Module (UPM) called Research Integrity and Ethics. 
For more information on this mandatory UPM, refer to SETU’s Graduate Studies Operational 
Procedures for Research Degrees. 
9. 
Research Misconduct  
 
SETU is committed to using transparent, robust, fair and timely processes to deal with 
allegations of research misconduct when they arise that adhere to the recommendations 
outlined in the National Forum on Research Integrity Guidelines for the Investigation of

2024) https://www.iua.ie/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/National-Policy-Statement-on-Ensuring-Research-

Misconduct in Research. SETU researchers should also refer to SETU’s Procedures for 
Managing Allegations of Misconduct in Research for more information on how to submit a 
complaint related to alleged research misconduct and the procedural details involved in an 
investigation into potential research misconduct. See Section 5 in this document for a full 
definition of research misconduct. 
 
Any postgraduate student, researcher, individual or external body (e.g. a funding agency or a 
publisher) who believes that an act of research misconduct has occurred or is occurring should 
make a complaint in writing through the completion and submission of a Complaint Form to 
SETU’s RIO at research.integrity@setu.ie. The complaint form can be found here. 
 
Any postgraduate student, researcher, individual or external body receiving an allegation 
about research misconduct should refer the complainant to the RIO. 
 
Breaches of research integrity or research misconduct take many forms and can be of varying 
seriousness. As outlined in the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity6 and the 
National Policy Statement on Ensuring Research Integrity in Ireland7, the most serious forms 
of research misconduct include: 
 
● 
Fabrication of data and results: i.e., making up results and recording or 
reporting them; 
● 
Falsification of data and results: i.e., manipulating research, materials, 
equipment or processes, or changing or omitting data or results such that 
the research is not accurately represented in the research record; 
● 
Plagiarism: i.e., the appropriation of another person’s ideas, processes, 
results, or words without giving appropriate credit, including those obtained 
through confidential review of others’ research proposals and manuscripts. 
Examples of these include:  
● Selectively excluding data from analysis;   
● Misinterpreting or altering data to obtain desired results (including 
inappropriate use of statistical methods); 
● Manipulating images and figures in publications;  
● Producing false data or results under pressure from a sponsor.

In addition to these, there are other types of unacceptable research practices which, while 
not as serious as the above, however, if repeated they may also constitute research 
misconduct. These practices include but are not confined to: 
 
● 
Data-related misconduct examples include: 
o 
Not preserving primary/raw data; 
o 
Poor data management, storage or preservation of primary data; 
o 
Not securely retaining other essential documentation such as 
completed informed consent forms. 
● 
Publication-related misconduct examples include: 
o 
Claiming undeserved authorship;  
o 
Denying authorship to contributors or unfairly ranking authors (e.g., 
denying first authorship where deserved);  
o 
Artificially proliferating publications (“salami-slicing” and “self 
plagiarism”); 
o 
Failure to correct the publication record; 
o 
Hiding the use of AI or automated tools in creating content or 
drafting publications; 
o 
Including authors without permission; 
o 
Selective or inaccurate citing to enhance importance of findings; 
o 
Establishing or supporting journals that undermine the quality 
control of research (‘predatory journals’, paper mills etc.); 
o 
Exaggerating the importance and practical applicability of findings. 
● 
Personal misconduct in the research setting could include:  
o 
Inappropriate personal behaviour; 
o 
Harassment, bullying; 
o 
Inadequate supervision, mentoring, counselling of researchers; 
o 
Insensitivity to social or cultural norms; 
o 
Misusing seniority to encourage violations of research integrity; 
o 
Delaying or inappropriately hampering the work of other 
researchers. 
● 
Research practice misconduct examples include: 
o 
Harmful, dangerous or unethical research methods;  
o 
Non-observation of health and safety standards; 
o 
Poor research design; 
o 
Experimental, analytical, computational errors; 
o 
Violation of human subject protocols;  
o 
Abuse of laboratory animals; 
o 
Concealing research misconduct by other researchers or by 
institutions.

● 
Financial and other malpractice: 
o 
Peer review abuse e.g., non-disclosure of conflict of interest, unfairly 
holding up a rival’s publication; 
o 
Misrepresenting credentials or publication record; 
o 
Misuse of research funds for unauthorised purchases or for personal 
gain; 
o 
Making an unsubstantiated or malicious misconduct allegation8. 
 
It is acknowledged that the examples of research misconduct listed here do not form an 
exhaustive list. Researchers are encouraged to consult with the RIO in cases where they have 
evidence or observed behaviour that may constitute research misconduct.        
10. 
Good Research Practices 
All SETU researchers should be familiar with and adhere to the SETU policies and procedures 
that govern the research process, as well as the other institutional policies of SETU. These 
policies are referenced throughout this document and the most recent versions can be 
accessed from the SETU policies webpage. 
 
10.1  Equality, Diversity and Inclusion  
  
SETU, and SETU researchers, commit to promoting and ensuring the values of equality, 
diversity and inclusion as outlined in SETU’s Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) Policy, 
SETU’s Strategic Plan, SETU’s EDI Strategic Plan and SETU’s Gender Equality Action Plan.   
 
All SETU researchers are valued members of the community and are assured the right of 
equitable, fair, and respectful treatment. SETU and SETU staff must ensure that laws 
prohibiting discrimination are complied with. Researchers should refer to SETU’s EDI Policy 
for full details of SETU’s commitment to the principles and promotion of equality, diversity 
and inclusion. 
           
10.2  Supervision and Mentoring 
 
Responsibility for ensuring that SETU researchers understand good research practice lies with 
all members of the research community, but particularly with Principal Investigators (PIs) and 
Supervisors.

Supervisors/PIs should ensure that researchers they are supervising are aware of SETU’s Code 
of Conduct for Responsible Research Practice and SETU’s Research Ethics Committee 
Operations and Application Guidance Documentation which provides guidance to those 
applying for ethical approval prior to conducting their research. 
 
In order to facilitate the overall progress of researchers they are supervising, Supervisors/PIs, 
together with the researcher, should develop a training plan to ensure they have the 
necessary understanding of good research practices and the skills necessary to successfully 
conduct their research. They should also ensure their researchers complete mandatory 
research integrity training (see Section 9 for further information). Supervisors must also 
complete mandatory research integrity training. 
 
Supervisors/PIs must ensure that their supervisees demonstrate good data management 
practices. This might include the development of a data management plan and the conduct 
of a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) if the researcher is collecting personal data. 
See Section 10.4 for more information on data management. 
 
Supervisors/PIs should refer to SETU’s Research Degree Regulations and SETU’s Graduate 
Studies Operational Procedures for Research Degrees and they should also familiarise 
themselves with QQI’s Ireland’s Framework of Good Practice for Research Degree 
Programmes9 and Ireland’s National Framework for Doctoral Education10 for further 
guidance. 
 
10.3  Management of Research Projects 
 
All research projects awarded to SETU must adhere to all requirements outlined by the 
funding body and the funding contract. For all self-funded projects and funded postgraduate 
research students, the policies and procedures of SETU must be adhered to. All marketing, 
project plans and reporting must be completed by the PI or project manager.  
 
Researchers must follow established SETU financial procedures, including those relating to 
procurement, and must practice economy in the use of resources. The PI and the research 
support functions of SETU must ensure that projects operate within their allocated budget,

and that no penalties are incurred by failure to meet sponsors’ requirements (each

All researchers within the project will be required to retain data and documentation for 
reports (both financial and technical), to include good record-keeping and data management.  
 
10.4  Data management and retention  
 
SETU researchers seeking guidance on data management, data protection, and data retention 
should refer to SETU’s comprehensive policies and procedures. The SETU Data Governance 
Policy provides direction on the classification, ownership and retention of data and 
information for SETU as well as clarifying accountability for data and information. The SETU 
Data Protection Policy ensures compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation 
(GDPR), safeguarding personal data in research projects. Additionally, the SETU Data 
Retention Policy provides clear guidelines on how long data should be retained and under 
what conditions it may be archived or deleted. These policies are designed to support 
researchers in maintaining ethical and legal standards in their work and can be accessed on 
SETU’s research integrity webpage. SETU researchers should also complete GDPR training. 
 
A Data Management Plan (DMP) is a formal document that outlines how you will handle the 
data you collect, generate, or use during your research project and it is a requirement of grant 
applications to many funding agencies. Researchers should refer to the SETU Data 
Management Guidance for information on devising a Data Management Plan (DMP) and how 
to devise one according to FAIR Data Principles11. PIs/supervisors have the overall 
responsibility to ensure the DMP is created and submitted to the funding agency. The 
PIs/supervisors will also ensure that researchers on a project adhere to data management 
plans, as they are responsible for both reporting and compliance. 
 
Under GDPR, researchers, who plan to collect personal data in their research, are required to 
complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before they collect and process the 
data. A DPIA is a risk assessment of the collection and processing of personal data and is a 
requirement for ethical approval of applications to the REC. It is the responsibility of 
supervisors/PIs to ensure that a DPIA is carried out and to support researchers with 
completing this. A DPIA template form is available here. 
 
Researchers should also refer to and comply with the SETU Data Inventory & Records 
Retention Schedule, which is a list outlining the retention periods for different types of

personal data collected and processed at SETU. This can be accessed here. Additionally, 
researchers should follow relevant specific guidance from funding bodies and any regulatory 
authorities in relation to retention of data. Data that has been retained over the minimum 
time can be discarded in line with the SETU Data Inventory & Records Retention Schedule.  
 
Researchers are encouraged to store their data in a secure repository for retrieval or audit 
purposes, and in line with open research principles as outlined in SETU’s Open Research 
Policy. 
 
If researchers or the PI with the responsibility for the research data leaves SETU for whatever 
reason, before the required period of data retention expires, they are required to ensure that 
the necessary arrangements for data retention are put in place.  It is the responsibility of the 
faculty to ensure adequate data management plans are in place.  
 
If postdoctoral researchers or research postgraduate students leave SETU, for whatever 
reason, before the required period of data retention expires, they must leave all research 
records (for example, laboratory books and digital data) with the PI or supervisor. Wherever 
possible, a copy of the original data will be retained in the department or research unit in 
which they were generated. The PI or supervisor must organise handover of data before the 
postdoctoral/postgraduate researchers leaves SETU. 
 
10.5 Intellectual Property 
 
The SETU Intellectual Property (IP) Policy clearly outlines the University’s approach to IP 
generated in and by the University. This policy sets out the rules that govern the creation, 
ownership, management, protection and exploitation of intellectual property developed by 
the SETU staff, students, and others participating in programmes carried out using the 
University facilities, know how, confidential information or intellectual property. SETU’s 
Technology Transfer Offices (TTO) provides support to staff, students and external 
collaborators on matters pertaining to IP. Researchers must adhere to the IP Policy, in 
addition to any specific contractual conditions of the research sponsor where applicable. For 
more guidance visit the webpage of the TTO. 
 
10.6 Publication & Dissemination  
 
SETU’s Authorship Policy outlines the guiding principles on authorship of publications arising 
from research activities, including collaborative work of SETU staff, researchers and students. 
SETU’s Authorship Policy provides guidance on the following: criteria for authorship; 
acknowledgement of the contribution of non-authors; order of authorship; responsibilities of 
authors; authorship dispute resolution; and issues relating to retention of data used in the

preparation of the papers /artefacts. Researchers should refer to the authorship policy to 
ensure integrity in authorship and publication. 
 
Prior to publication, researchers should refer to SETU’s Intellectual Property Policy and 
consult with the TTO, particularly in the case of collaborative research, and they shall refrain 
from publication or disclosure until any necessary IP protection has been secured. 
 
Ireland‘s transition to open research policy is outlined in the National Action Plan for Open 
Research12.  The plan foregrounds a theme of establishing a culture of open research, open 
access to research publications, enabling Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable 
(FAIR) research data and other outputs. SETU researchers should refer to SETU’s Open 
Research Policy, which states that researchers must adhere to the specific terms and 
conditions within contracts (e.g. European Research Council, EU funding) where it relates to 
the publication of research in an open access fashion. 
 
Researchers must make all reasonable attempts to present their research outputs to the 
academic community through peer-reviewed papers, books, presentations or other suitable 
media and, where appropriate, to the public.  As a signatory of the San Francisco Declaration 
on Research Assessment (DORA)13, SETU is committed to improving how research outputs are 
evaluated. Researchers are expected to ensure that their dissemination practices align with 
DORA principles, which emphasize the quality and impact of research over quantitative 
metrics such as journal impact factors.  
      
10.7 Conflicts of Interest 
  
SETU Researchers have an obligation to manage or avoid ethical, legal, financial or other 
conflicts of interest and to ensure that their activities and interests do not conflict with their 
obligations to SETU. It is the responsibility of SETU Researchers to identify and declare any 
potential, actual or perceived conflicts of interest, whether financial, beneficial, personal, 
ethical, legal, or other, so that this does not become a complicating or actionable issue. 
Researchers should refer to SETU’s Conflict of Interest Policy for detailed guidance on this 
matter and how to notify SETU in relation to a conflict of interest in the context of research.  
 
10.8 Export Control  
 
The EU operates a system of controls on the export of sensitive items from member states, 
which form part of a global framework designed to prevent the proliferation of weapons of

mass destruction, to support global security, prevent terrorism and to protect human rights. 
Export controls include licensing requirements for certain sensitive goods or export 
restrictions in respect of certain destination countries or end-users. Dual-Use Regulation is EU 
legislation which lists the dual-use items subject to control and requiring authorisation for 
export outside the EU. Dual-use export controls govern activities involving items (materials) 
equipment, software, and technologies which can be used for both civil and military purposes. 
 
As outlined in SETU’s Export Controls Policy SETU researchers must understand and comply 
with Irish law14 and EU regulations on export controls. If an SETU researcher exports a listed 
item or exports technical assistance/knowhow etc. relating to a listed item, the researcher 
must first obtain a licence from the national competent authority with responsibility for 
administering and enforcing these controls, the Trade Licensing & Control Unit of the 
Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE). Whilst academic freedom is a 
fundamental right guaranteed by the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, 
that does not exempt researchers and universities from complying with these regulations.  
 
It is the responsibility of each individual researcher to ensure that they do not export 
controlled items without an appropriate licence. Researchers are expected to familiarise 
themselves with SETU’s Export Controls Policy and refer to the Government of Ireland Export 
Licensing and Control Information for Exporters. For the full list of all export controls covered 
by European legislation, see the Common Military List15. The European Commission 
Recommendation 2021/170016 also provides guidelines for universities on how they can 
comply with export controls.  
 
Researchers should contact the SETU Office for Research, Innovation and Impact (RII) or the 
TTO if they have any queries or require support regarding exporting goods or knowledge. 
Information is also available on a dedicated SETU export controls webpage. Training is also 
available for all SETU researchers through a specialist module on Export Controls as part of 
the Research Integrity (RI) Training, training that is mandatory for all SETU researchers (see 
Section 8 Research Integrity Training). Additional training and supports can be found on 
SETU’s export controls webpage.

10.9 AI in Research 
 
Researchers must be transparent and acknowledge their use of AI tools and Generative AI in 
their research. Researchers must always be accountable for the integrity and reliability of any 
content generated by Gen AI or with the support of AI tools. Researchers must always 
acknowledge their use of AI and reference any content produced by AI in publications, peer 
review, grant applications and evaluations of research proposals. Any use of AI in the research 
process—including, but not limited to, literature search, methods, data collection, data 
analysis, writing assistance, translation or image generation—should be appropriately 
acknowledged in publications or any other research outputs.  
 
As SETU does not yet have a formal policy on the use of AI in research, researchers can refer 
to SETU’s Student Guidelines on the Use of Gen AI and SETU library’s tutorial Generative AI 
and Prompt Literacy Guide for Students. SETU’s Moodle and Blackboard have dedicated 
Generative AI Hubs with resources available for students and staff. Researchers should refer 
to the EU’s Living Guidelines on the Responsible Use of Generative AI in Research (pages 6-
7). In preparing publications, grant applications or writing peer reviews, researchers must 
refer to the most up to date guidance from the individual publishers and funding agencies 
whose guidance is constantly evolving.
